source_acquisition.search_note: The inventory row lists ttsds/pipeline as exact_visual_source and proposes six scripts. The PDF explicitly links github.com/ttsds/pipeline, which gh resolves to https://github.com/ttsds/daisy; gh metadata describes it as the multilingual TTSDS2 benchmark pipeline. The README/tree and the locally acquired scripts/figures files are Daisy data-summary, flower-plot, source/filtering and speaker-similarity generators, not exact sources for PDF Figures 1–8 or Tables 1–8; local acquisition lacks the inventory's create_flower.py. gh title search returns only ttsds/daisy and strict code search in that repository returns no TTSDS2 visual generator. GPT-SoVITS and Bark are evaluated systems cited in Appendix Table 6, not author-linked visual sources. No exact plot/table/LaTeX/notebook/data source was found, so the public repository is recorded as repository_without_visual_source rather than exact_visual_source.

paper_style.palette_strategy: Tables 2, 3 and Appendix Figure 7 use a shared pale green-to-pale red correlation/ranking palette; Figure 2 uses four domain colors with redundant marker shapes; Figure 3 uses a purple-to-yellow-green categorical box palette; Figure 8 uses pale green nearest-neighbor edges; Appendix Figures 4–6 are grayscale screenshots. Tables otherwise rely on black text, booktabs-like rules and bold/symbol cues.
paper_style.vector_raster_mix: All 20 pages were rendered at 200 dpi. PDF font/object inspection and pdfimages -list show Figures 1–3, 7 and 8 and all tables as primarily vector objects; Figures 4–6 are embedded RGB/alpha raster screenshots with vector captions. The visual system is therefore mostly vector with a small raster interface appendix.
paper_style.style_consistency: Nimbus Roman No9 L, Computer Modern math and black/white table rules are stable across main text and appendix. Plot internals switch to ArialMT or DejaVu Sans, while the listening-test screenshots use an unspecified web sans-serif raster. Color semantics are locally consistent for Figure 2 and Tables 2/3/Figure 7 but not globally shared with Figure 3 or Figure 8.

figures.label: Figure 1

caption.text: Figure 1: Distribution of F0 in TTSDS for ground-truth, synthetic, and noise datasets.

color.semantic_mapping: Noise, Ground Truth and Synthetic are black/gray curves; white is the plot background.

encodings.line: Noise dashed, Ground Truth solid, Synthetic dotted

figures.data_and_statistics: The plot is a one-dimensional pitch-distribution illustration, with no reported sample count, unit of aggregation, KDE/bandwidth definition, or uncertainty. It shows a narrow Noise peak against multi-modal Ground Truth and Synthetic curves.
figures.evidence_relation: Section 2 frames TTSDS2 as matching the empirical synthetic distribution to real speech while remaining distinct from noise; this Figure 1 is the visual intuition for the W2 construction. Table 1 specifies the factor feature set, while Tables 2–3 carry system-level evidence.
design_strengths: Dashed, solid and dotted lines make the three distributions distinguishable without color.
The Hz and density axes make the intended one-dimensional feature explicit.
The in-plot legend stays near the right tail without covering the main peaks.
design_weaknesses: The caption does not state the density-estimation method, sample range or smoothing choice.
A single F0 feature cannot represent the full four-factor metric.
The legend is inside the plotting area and the tail shapes can be over-interpreted without the method text.
figures.reusable_pattern: Use one common coordinate system and line-style-only roles for real, synthetic and noise distributions before introducing a distributional distance.

figures.label: Figure 2

caption.text: Figure 2: Correlation of three representative objective metrics with human MOS across the four datasets. Each colour/marker denotes a domain. Solid line = overall least-squares fit; dashed/dotted lines = domain-specific fits; each with corresponding Pearson r.

color.semantic_mapping: Clean=red diamond, Noisy=orange triangle, Wild=green square, Kids=blue circle; dark line is the overall fit.

encodings.x: one of TTSDS, SQUIM or X-Vector objective scores
encodings.shape: domain marker: diamond, triangle, square or circle
encodings.line: overall solid least-squares fit and domain-specific dashed/dotted fits
encodings.facet: three metric panels: TTSDS, SQUIM and X-Vector
encodings.text: per-panel Pearson r annotations and metric titles

figures.data_and_statistics: Each panel contains roughly 20 systems in each of four domains (about 80 aggregated system-domain points), with domain-specific and pooled least-squares fits. The plotted statistic is Pearson r for the fits; no error bars, intervals, seed repeats or sample-level denominator are shown.
figures.evidence_relation: The scatter panels expand Table 3's rank correlations into score geometry. The paper describes TTSDS2 as more continuous and SQUIM/X-Vector as showing clustering, while explicitly leaving overfitting as a possibility rather than a tested mechanism.
design_strengths: The three metrics share a MOS y-axis and a fixed domain encoding, supporting direct visual comparison.
Marker shape, color, line style and legend jointly expose pooled versus domain-specific structure.
Pearson r annotations prevent the regression lines from being the only quantitative cue.
design_weaknesses: Four-domain point overlap and multiple fits are dense at the page scale.
Domain-specific dash/dot semantics are only partially explicit and become difficult in grayscale.
No uncertainty or repeated-fit display supports the apparent differences between correlations.
figures.reusable_pattern: Use matched domain markers and a shared y-axis across metric panels, then overlay one pooled fit and domain fits with a caption that names every line role.

figures.label: Figure 3

caption.text: Figure 3: TTSDS2 scores across 14 languages. n indicates the number of systems per language.

color.semantic_mapping: Purple-to-yellow-green box fills distinguish the 14 language groups; pale gray band and black x markers provide the Ground Truth reference.

encodings.x: 14 language categories with n shown in each label
encodings.color: language-group box fill in a sequential visual palette
encodings.shape: box/whisker, hollow outlier circle and Ground Truth x marker
encodings.text: rotated language labels and n counts; Ground Truth legend

figures.data_and_statistics: The figure displays language-level boxplot distributions for the multilingual benchmark; n ranges from 2 to 20 systems per language. Boxes encode distribution summaries, whiskers and hollow circles expose spread/outliers, and black x marks show Ground Truth. A pale gray horizontal band is visible, but its statistical meaning is not defined by the caption.
figures.evidence_relation: Section 4.2 uses this benchmark to extend evaluation beyond English and to motivate the Uriel+ typological-distance proxy. The figure supports the observation that lower-resource languages have lower scores, but there is no multilingual gold MOS and therefore no direct human-quality claim.
design_strengths: One y-scale exposes both within-language spread and between-language location.
Explicit n labels make unequal system coverage visible.
Ground Truth x markers give a common reference without a second axis.
design_weaknesses: Fourteen rotated labels and small n values are crowded at the rendered size.
The gray reference band is not explained, and the sequential color order can be mistaken for a quantitative axis.
Unequal n values make box stability difficult to judge; no raw points or uncertainty around the language summaries are shown.
figures.reusable_pattern: Use categorical boxplots with n labels and a clearly defined reference marker for multilingual slices; define any background reference band in the caption.

figures.label: Figure 4

caption.text: Figure 4: Interface for Mean Opinion Score (MOS) listening tests.

color.semantic_mapping: Dark audio player, light Likert cards, gray labels and white canvas form a grayscale listening-test interface.

encodings.shape: radio circles and rectangular response cards

figures.data_and_statistics: A single embedded screenshot shows one audio player, a naturalness prompt, and five response cards from 1 (bad) to 5 (excellent). It is an interface artifact rather than a statistical plot and contains no sample, denominator or uncertainty.
figures.evidence_relation: Appendix B.1 defines the MOS input used by the listening tests summarized in Tables 2, 3 and 7; the screenshot makes the five-point response contract concrete but does not expose assignment, randomization or attention-check state.
design_strengths: Player, prompt and response scale follow a simple top-to-bottom reading order.
The five options are equally spaced and visibly selectable.
Grayscale presentation avoids a color-only response code.
design_weaknesses: The screenshot is small after paper scaling and does not show a selected/submitted state.
Caption does not say that this is a single-sample naturalness task.
Randomization and quality-control elements described in prose are absent from the visual.
figures.reusable_pattern: Pair a compact, high-resolution interface crop with the exact response scale used by the result tables, while documenting interaction states separately.

figures.label: Figure 5

caption.text: Figure 5: Interface for Comparison MOS (CMOS) listening tests.

color.semantic_mapping: Dark paired players, light seven-point response cards, gray labels and white canvas form a grayscale comparison interface.

encodings.shape: seven rectangular response cards with radio circles
encodings.text: Clip A/B labels and −3 to +3 relative-naturalness wording

figures.data_and_statistics: A paired screenshot shows two audio players, Clip A and Clip B labels, and seven ordered response cards from 3 (A is much better) through 0 (about the same) to −3 (A is much worse). It has no statistical data or uncertainty.
figures.evidence_relation: The screenshot is the interface counterpart of the CMOS scale described in Appendix B.1 and used in Tables 2, 3 and 7. It makes the comparison direction explicit but cannot establish actual order balancing or listener assignment.
design_strengths: The two input players are aligned horizontally and named before the question.
All seven response directions are written in the cards, reducing sign ambiguity.
The layout is visually parallel to the MOS interface.
design_weaknesses: Long seven-point labels wrap into narrow cards and become small at page scale.
No selected state, randomization cue or submission feedback is shown.
Caption omits the −3/+3 direction, so the static screenshot needs Appendix B.1 prose.
figures.reusable_pattern: For pairwise subjective metrics, show both input controls and the full signed response scale in one aligned crop, then state the sign convention in the caption.

figures.label: Figure 6

caption.text: Figure 6: Interface for Speaker Similarity MOS (SMOS) listening tests.

color.semantic_mapping: Dark paired players, light five-point response cards, gray labels and white canvas form a grayscale speaker-similarity interface.

encodings.shape: radio circles and five rectangular response cards
encodings.text: Clip A/B and speaker similarity question

figures.data_and_statistics: A paired screenshot shows two players, Clip A/B labels, a speaker-similarity prompt and five response cards from 1 (bad) to 5 (excellent). It contains no data, aggregation or uncertainty.
figures.evidence_relation: The interface is the input contract for SMOS, which the paper describes as a voice-cloning speaker-similarity test and aggregates in Tables 2, 3 and 7. It complements Figure 4's single-sample MOS and Figure 5's signed CMOS comparison.
design_strengths: The A/B structure and five-point scale are immediately visible.
Shared gray UI language makes the three listening-test interfaces easy to compare.
Bold keywords distinguish the speaker-similarity question from surrounding text.
design_weaknesses: The screenshot does not show which clip is the reference speaker or how order is randomized.
Caption does not state the speaker-reference relation or the 1–5 interpretation.
Small raster text limits accessibility in the printed appendix.
figures.reusable_pattern: Keep MOS, CMOS and SMOS interface crops geometrically consistent and change only the task-specific prompt and response scale.

figures.label: Figure 7

caption.text: Figure 7: Significant (p < 0.05) Spearman correlation heatmaps between metrics.

color.semantic_mapping: Significant positive-to-negative Spearman correlations use green-to-red diverging cell fills; white/blank cells are non-significant or unfilled. Each panel has a −1 to 1 colorbar.

encodings.x: categorical metric labels in fixed order
encodings.y: same metric vocabulary on the row axis
encodings.color: sign and magnitude of significant Spearman correlation
encodings.text: cell correlations, metric-family labels and colorbar ticks

figures.data_and_statistics: Each panel uses approximately 22 metrics on both axes, with only significant cells populated and coefficients printed in very small text. The displayed values are Spearman correlations; the figure gives p < 0.05 as the inclusion rule but not the test form, denominator or multiplicity correction.
figures.evidence_relation: Appendix E expands Table 3 from metric-to-human-MOS cells to the complete objective/subjective metric relationship. It supports the domain-shift discussion around TTSDS2, SQUIM, RawNet3 and negative MCD/WER/PESQ associations; blank cells are not evidence of zero correlation.
design_strengths: The same metric ordering and color scale make in-domain and cross-domain patterns comparable.
Metric-family labels group subjective, distributional, MOS-prediction, speaker, signal and ASR metrics.
Colorbars and printed values jointly communicate direction and approximate magnitude.
design_weaknesses: Twenty-two labels and 4–5 pt coefficients are extremely dense at paper scale.
The caption does not explain the color bins, blank-cell semantics or whether the second panel is pooled.
Positive/negative sign is difficult to recover in grayscale, and significance filtering can be mistaken for a complete matrix.
figures.reusable_pattern: Use fixed metric order and matched diverging heatmaps for domain shifts, but define blank cells, color limits, denominator and multiplicity policy in the caption or table note.

figures.label: Figure 8

caption.text: Figure 8: Multidimensional scaling (MDS) distance plots between languages (left to right) for i) Uriel+ typological distances ii) TTSDS2 without multilingual changes iii) multilingual TTSDS2. The three closest neighbors of each language are connected via lines.

color.semantic_mapping: Pale green edges connect three nearest neighbors; black/dark node labels and white canvas carry the language identities.

encodings.line: edges connecting each language to its three closest neighbors

figures.data_and_statistics: Three panels reuse 14 language nodes (AR, DE, EN, ES, FR, IT, JA, KO, NL, PL, PT, RU, TR and ZH) and draw nearest-neighbor edges. MDS coordinates have no axis, scale or uncertainty; the graph is a qualitative comparison of neighborhood structure rather than a numeric distance plot.
figures.evidence_relation: Section 4.2 interprets ground-truth language dataset distances as a proxy and compares them with Uriel+ typological distances. The figure visualizes that proxy relationship, not multilingual human MOS or a language phylogeny.
design_strengths: The node vocabulary is fixed across panels, so neighborhood changes are easy to scan.
Connecting only three nearest neighbors limits edge density relative to a complete graph.
Direct two-letter labels make nodes identifiable without a legend.
design_weaknesses: No panel titles, coordinate scale or numeric distance legend are drawn inside the panels.
Pale edges cross and are hard to quantify; the left-to-right mapping must be retained from the caption.
The caption does not expand the language abbreviations or state the MDS dimensionality/normalization.
figures.reusable_pattern: For multiple distance embeddings, keep node identities and layout vocabulary fixed, connect a small nearest-neighbor set, and add panel titles plus an abbreviation key.

tables.label: Table 1

caption.text: Table 1: Feature set used for TTSDS compared to TTSDS2.

tables.uncertainty: No uncertainty or numeric statistic is shown.
tables.data_and_statistics: A five-row factor comparison lists old TTSDS features and updated TTSDS2 features; Environment is explicitly marked '(Factor removed)'. Feature names and cited model families are the data encoding.
tables.evidence_relation: Section 2 factorised metric definition → Table 1 feature changes → Table 3 correlations and Tables 4–5/Appendix Table 8 factor diagnostics.
design_strengths: Old/new columns make retained, replaced and removed features visible.
Factor labels provide stable method vocabulary for later tables.
Black-and-white rules remain legible without palette dependence.
design_weaknesses: Citation text competes with feature names and creates multi-line dense cells.
There is no explicit new/removed marker beyond prose and the removed-factor text.
Caption does not say that feature selection preceded correlation experiments.
tables.reusable_pattern: Present a versioned factor-by-feature table with deletion stated inside the cell and a stable factor vocabulary reused in result tables.

tables.label: Table 2

caption.text: Table 2: Mean over datasets of MOS, CMOS, SMOS and the corresponding TTSDS2 score.

tables.uncertainty: MOS, CMOS and SMOS cells show mean ± an undefined dispersion statistic; TTSDS2 is a point score without ±. The paper does not define the ± statistic in the caption.
tables.data_and_statistics: Ground Truth plus 20 systems are summarized over four English domains. MOS/CMOS/SMOS means keep two decimal places and TTSDS2 keeps two decimals; higher/lower cells receive pale green/pink/gray fills.
tables.evidence_relation: Four-domain listening-test averages → Table 2 cross-domain summary → Table 3 domain-specific rank correlations and Appendix Table 7 raw slices.
design_strengths: Human and objective metrics sit on the same system row for direct ranking inspection.
The Ground Truth row is separated at the top and exact numeric values remain visible over fill colors.
Compact width preserves the main comparison in the results page.
design_weaknesses: Cell colors mix different scales/directions and their thresholds are not defined.
The ± statistic and denominator are absent, and TTSDS2 has no uncertainty counterpart.
Six-point table text is difficult to read without zooming.
tables.reusable_pattern: Use one row per system to align subjective and objective summaries, but document color normalization and the definition of any dispersion symbol.

tables.label: Table 3
tables.uncertainty: Point estimates only; no interval, standard error, per-cell denominator, p-value or multiplicity annotation is displayed.
tables.data_and_statistics: The table reports Spearman ρ across 18 metrics, four domain column groups and MOS/CMOS/SMOS subcolumns; each cell is a two-decimal rank correlation. The caption defines four color intervals from −1 to 1.
tables.evidence_relation: The central cross-domain ranking claim is reported here; Figure 2 adds score geometry, Table 4 tests aggregation generalization, and Appendix Figure 7 expands pairwise metric relationships.
design_strengths: Two-level domain/subjective header makes the 12 estimands explicit.
TTSDS2 and TTSDS are placed first for direct version comparison.
Numeric values remain available even when color intervals are coarse.
design_weaknesses: 18 × 12 values are dense, and a four-bin scale hides fine differences such as 0.50 versus 0.70.
No per-cell denominator or uncertainty is shown.
Color remains important for rapid sign/magnitude scanning despite printed numbers.
tables.reusable_pattern: Use a fixed domain × subjective-task header and retain exact coefficients in cells; treat the heat color as navigation rather than the statistic itself.

tables.label: Table 4

caption.text: Table 4: Leave-One-Out Cross-Validation (Generalisation). Evaluation on a held-out domain after training on the other three.

tables.uncertainty: LOOCV point scores only; no interval, repeat or per-domain sample denominator is shown.
tables.data_and_statistics: Four held-out domains compare Simple Mean (Baseline) with Learned Weights (LOOCV), with three decimal places and row-wise bolding of the larger score.
tables.evidence_relation: Section 3.5 equal-weight design choice → Table 4 held-out aggregation comparison → Table 5 coefficient instability.
design_strengths: Held-out domain is a natural row key and makes the 3-of-4 comparison immediately visible.
Consistent precision and row-wise bolding reduce lookup effort.
The narrow table fits beside Table 5 so performance and weight diagnostics are adjacent.
design_weaknesses: Training domain set is implicit rather than listed in each row.
The score/estimand is not named in the table itself.
Single point values do not show variability across domains or fitting repeats.
tables.reusable_pattern: Put held-out condition on rows and baseline/proposed aggregation on columns, with explicit fit and evaluation definitions in the caption.

tables.label: Table 5

caption.text: Table 5: Instability of learned weights. Optimal coefficients vary drastically by training domain, occasionally becoming negative.

tables.uncertainty: Coefficients are point estimates; no standard errors, intervals, training sample counts or coefficient constraints are shown.
tables.data_and_statistics: Five training conditions are rows and four factor coefficients (Gen., Speak., Pros., Intel.) are columns, all to three decimals; negative coefficients are retained rather than clipped.
tables.evidence_relation: Table 4 learned-weight LOOCV → Table 5 training-domain coefficient variation → simple unweighted mean as the regularizing design decision.
design_strengths: Factor columns align with Table 1 and make sign changes easy to scan.
Negative coefficients visibly expose instability rather than hiding it in an aggregate score.
Side-by-side placement with Table 4 ties coefficient behavior to held-out performance.
design_weaknesses: Factor abbreviations are not fully self-explanatory.
No scale or uncertainty helps interpret the word 'drastically'.
The fitting target and regularization details are not encoded in the table.
tables.reusable_pattern: Report learned weights next to held-out scores and preserve negative values so domain overfit is directly inspectable.

tables.label: Table 6

caption.text: Table 6: Open-source TTS systems, prior evaluation, and results for each system relative to ground-truth (GT) speech: † = accompanied by publication; ∗ = third-party implementation; Parity column: Reported MOS/CMOS are close to GT (∼), surpassing GT (>) or below GT (<)

tables.uncertainty: No current score uncertainty is shown. Objective/Subjective are checkmark presence flags and Parity is an ordinal symbol, not a numeric effect estimate.
tables.data_and_statistics: Twenty rows list System, Year, Objective, Subjective and Parity. Dagger/star provenance, checkmarks and ∼/>/< parity symbols encode prior evidence and reported relation to GT.
tables.evidence_relation: Section 1.2 selected-systems frame → Table 6 provenance/catalog → Table 2 current unified evaluation; the table distinguishes external reports from current measurements.
design_strengths: The caption defines every special symbol and separates prior evaluation from parity.
A single page-width catalog provides a useful reproduction index for the 20-system benchmark.
Year and provenance symbols make the selection window inspectable.
design_weaknesses: System names and citations are tightly packed, especially for multi-paper rows.
Reported parity is not the same as the current Table 2 score and requires contextual reading.
No summary counts or confidence/quality field accompanies the checkmarks.
tables.reusable_pattern: Catalog benchmark systems with source, date, prior evidence and comparison status, while keeping external reports distinct from the new experiment.

tables.label: Table 7

caption.text: Table 7: Listening test results in terms of MOS, CMOS and SMOS relative to ground truth speech.

tables.uncertainty: Every domain/metric cell is mean ± an undefined dispersion statistic; the caption does not define the ± term or listener/sample denominator.
tables.data_and_statistics: A rotated wide table expands Ground Truth plus 20 systems across four domain column groups (Clean, Noisy, Wild, Kids), each with MOS, CMOS and SMOS. Means and ± values use two decimals; selected synthetic-system cells are bold.
tables.evidence_relation: Table 2's cross-domain summary → Table 7 raw domain slices → Table 3 correlations and Figure 4–6 listening interfaces.
design_strengths: The raw domain × metric slices preserve heterogeneity lost in Table 2.
Two-level column grouping supports horizontal system tracking across all four domains.
Ground Truth is kept as a visible baseline row.
design_weaknesses: Rotation and very small type make lookup slow and increase orientation errors.
Bold selection rule and ± statistic are not stated in the caption.
Mixed signed CMOS and positive MOS/SMOS columns need careful semantic reading.
tables.reusable_pattern: Move a complete domain × metric slice to an appendix wide table and state the dispersion and highlighting rules explicitly.

tables.label: Table 8

caption.text: Table 8: Pearson correlation (r) between each factor and MOS.

tables.uncertainty: Pearson r point estimates only; no sample count, p-value, interval or multiplicity information is displayed.
tables.data_and_statistics: Four dataset rows and four factor columns report two-decimal factor–MOS Pearson correlations; the largest value in each row is bold.
tables.evidence_relation: Table 1 factor design → Table 8 component correlations → Table 4–5 aggregation/generalization and Appendix Figure 7 metric-family analysis.
design_strengths: Compact factor × domain matrix makes complementarity visible.
Complete factor names are used in the header, avoiding the abbreviations in Table 5.
Row-wise bolding gives a quick dominant-factor cue while preserving all values.
design_weaknesses: Pearson r is different from the main Spearman ρ and the distinction is not in the table title beyond the coefficient name.
No sample size or significance annotation supports the component comparisons.
Row maxima can be mistaken for a universal factor ranking.
tables.reusable_pattern: Use a small factor-by-domain matrix to decompose an aggregate metric, and label the correlation type and denominator in the table note.

cross_object_system.visual_narrative: Table 1 defines the factor/feature interface; Figure 1 supplies the F0 distribution intuition; Table 2 summarizes cross-domain human/objective scores; Table 3 and Figure 2 expose rank and score geometry; Tables 4–5 test equal weighting and learned-weight instability; Figure 3 extends the benchmark to 14 languages. Appendix Table 6, Figures 4–6, Table 7, Table 8, Figure 7 and Figure 8 then provide system provenance, listening interfaces, raw domain slices, factor decomposition, full metric correlations and multilingual distance structure.
cross_object_system.caption_system: Captions are mostly short, regular serif sentences without bold conclusion headings. Figure 2 and Table 6 provide the most complete encoding keys; Table 2/3/7, Figure 3 and Figures 4–6 leave aggregation, ± definitions or protocol details to surrounding prose. Figure 8 clearly maps the three panels and nearest-neighbor edges.
cross_object_system.table_header_system: Headers follow factor × version (Table 1), domain × subjective metric (Table 3), held-out domain × aggregation (Table 4), and training domain × factor coefficient (Table 5). Appendix Table 6 uses symbol-defined status columns, Table 7 expands to four domain column groups, and Table 8 reuses the factor vocabulary from Table 1.
cross_object_system.method_result_ablation_link: Table 1/Figure 1's distributional factor interface leads to Table 2 aggregate results, Table 3/Figure 2 rank and fit evidence, Table 4–5 aggregation ablations, and Table 8 component correlations. Figure 3 and Figure 8 are multilingual benchmark/proxy extensions; Figure 7 is a metric-family robustness diagnostic.
cross_object_system.main_appendix_link: Main pages p.3, p.5 and p.7–9 carry the feature interface, F0 example, main scores, correlations, LOOCV and multilingual boxplot. Appendix pages p.15–20 expand system provenance, MOS/CMOS/SMOS interfaces, raw domain values, factor correlations, metric heatmaps, compute context and language-distance visualization.
cross_object_system.typography_consistency: Captions and tables consistently use Nimbus Roman No9 L with Computer Modern math and mostly 6–10 pt table text. Plot internals use PDF-embedded ArialMT/DejaVu Sans and the screenshots use raster UI text, so the system is coherent at the document level but not a single figure-font family.
cross_object_system.color_consistency: The pale green/pale red scale is reused between Table 2, Table 3 and Figure 7, while Figure 2's domain colors are reinforced by markers. Figure 3's sequential fills and Figure 8's pale green edges are local roles; Figure 1 and Figures 4–6 remain grayscale. Figure 7 is the least grayscale-safe object because color carries correlation sign/magnitude across dense cells.

most_reusable_patterns: Use a factor × old/new feature table to define a metric interface before showing results.
Use a line-style-only real/synthetic/noise distribution example to make a distance construction concrete.
Pair a domain × subjective correlation table with fixed-domain marker scatter panels and pooled/domain fits.
Place held-out aggregation scores next to learned coefficient diagnostics so overfit is visible rather than hidden.
Keep multilingual distributions, raw domain slices and full metric heatmaps as appendix expansions of concise main tables.
highest_value_objects: Table 3: the central four-domain × three-subjective-score rank-correlation matrix.
Figure 2: pooled and domain-specific score geometry for TTSDS, SQUIM and X-Vector.
Tables 4–5: paired evidence for equal-weight generalization and learned-weight instability.
Figure 3: language-level score distributions with explicit system counts and Ground Truth markers.
Appendix Table 7, Table 8 and Figure 7: raw domain heterogeneity, factor decomposition and metric-family context.
failure_patterns: Point estimates commonly omit seeds, repeats, denominators and intervals; Table 2 and Table 7 leave ± undefined.
Table 3 and Figure 7 report p < 0.05 significance without complete test/multiplicity context.
Figure 3's gray reference band is undefined and its language labels are crowded; Figure 8 lacks scales, panel titles and an abbreviation key.
Figure 7's 22 × 22 matrices use tiny coefficients and color-dependent sign encoding; Figures 4–6 are not self-contained listening protocols.
The explicitly linked ttsds/pipeline repository identity is verified, but its current Daisy visual scripts do not reproduce this PDF's Figures 1–8 or Tables 1–8.
final_judgment.one_sentence_visual_strategy: The paper defines TTSDS2 with a feature comparison and F0 distribution, supports cross-domain ranking with a correlation matrix and multi-panel scatter, then uses equal-weight ablations, multilingual boxplots and appendix raw/heatmap/MDS objects to expose generalization and evidence boundaries.
